title: The Stage-Fright Singer
twist: Usually 'she's nervous' is the lazy wrong answer in these cases. Here the nerves really are the cause — the job is to explain how a thought becomes a racing heart, sweaty palms and a dry mouth all at once.
briefing: Ava, 15, is about to sing a solo at the school concert. Standing in the wings her heart is racing, her palms are damp, her mouth is dry and her hands shake slightly. She has not moved a muscle. Ten minutes after the song ends she feels completely calm.
question: Why does a body that is standing still act like it is sprinting — and then switch off?

clues.title: Racing heart, standing still
clues.text: Pulse about 120 while standing perfectly still backstage. Her resting pulse is usually about 70.
clues.shows: a heart racing with no physical effort to explain it

clues.title: Damp palms, dry mouth
clues.text: Her palms are sweaty but her mouth is dry — two opposite things happening at the same moment.
clues.shows: several different body systems changing at once

clues.title: The thought, not the room
clues.text: The room is cool and quiet. It started the moment the teacher said 'you're next' — before anything physical happened.
clues.shows: that a thought, not the surroundings, set it off

clues.title: Calm in ten minutes
clues.text: Ten minutes after the last note: pulse back near 75, hands steady, mouth normal.
clues.shows: everything settling together once the moment passed

hypotheses.text: She has been running around backstage.
hypotheses.flaw: She was standing still — and exercise would not give her a dry mouth or make everything switch off in ten minutes.

hypotheses.text: Her brain judged the solo as a big moment and released adrenaline, which gets the whole body ready to act at once — heart, sweat, mouth — and fades within minutes when the moment passes.
The stage lights are making her hot.
hypotheses.flaw: Heat makes the whole body sweat, not just the palms, and it does not dry your mouth or start at the words 'you're next' in a cool room.

hypotheses.text: She is coming down with something.
hypotheses.flaw: An illness does not arrive at 'you're next' and leave ten minutes after the song.

prediction.prompt: As a moment feels bigger — from relaxing at home, to a class presentation, to a solo on stage — what happens to Ava's heart rate while she stands still?

concepts.label: the brain judges the moment
concepts.hint: What set it off — the room, or something in her head?

concepts.label: adrenaline is released
concepts.hint: What chemical message carries the alarm?

concepts.label: heart speeds up
concepts.hint: Which organ reacted first and most obviously?

concepts.label: many systems at once
concepts.hint: How many different things changed together?

concepts.label: fades when it's over
concepts.hint: What happened once the song was finished?

transfer.context: Eli is waiting to take a driving test. Sitting in the parked car he notices his heart thumping, his hands clammy on the wheel and a dry mouth.
options: The car's heater is on too high.
His brain has judged the test as a big moment and released adrenaline, so his heart, sweat glands and mouth all respond at once.
He pulled a muscle getting into the car.
transfer.retryHint: Sitting still but the body is revving — which of Ava's clues says the trigger was a thought?
transfer.explanation: Eli has not moved, but his brain has decided the test matters, and adrenaline does the rest: faster heart, clammy hands, dry mouth. It is the same alarm system as Ava's, and like hers it will fade within minutes of the test ending.

takeaway: Your brain has an alarm system. When it judges a moment as big, one chemical — adrenaline — changes heart, sweat and mouth all at once to get you ready, and it fades within minutes when the moment passes.
